text: {"summary":"Selling 50% of the whole portfolio to cash would raise the cash share from 0.4% to 50.2%, while the total portfolio value stays at $657,234. In the crash replays, the portfolio’s largest falls are smaller after the trade.","points":["The largest company holdings shown—JNJ, PG, and KO—would each be about half their previous share. Cash would become the largest sector allocation at 50.7%, while Bonds would fall from 26.7% to 13.3% and Technology from 18.8% to 9.4%.","In the past crash replays, the worst fall changes from 40.3% ($264,672) to 21.8% ($143,230) for the 2008 financial crisis; from 24.6% ($161,961) to 12.9% ($84,476) for the Covid crash; and from 21.5% ($141,277) to 11.2% ($73,378) for 2022.","In the 2008–09 crisis, SPY fell 55.2% from peak to bottom. After the bottom on March 9, 2009, it gained 71.9% over 1 year and 114.3% over 3 years, and took 41.3 months to recover. Someone who sold near that bottom would have been out during those subsequent gains; someone who bought near the peak would have experienced the fall.","In the Covid crash, SPY fell 33.7% from peak to bottom. After the bottom on March 23, 2020, it gained 77.5% over 1 year and 84.6% over 3 years, and took 4.6 months to recover. Someone who sold near that bottom would have been out during those subsequent gains; someone who bought near the peak would have experienced the fall."]}
